claim: Prior exposure to aversive stimuli or stressors changes behavioral responses to negative- and positive-value predictive cues.
source: For example, prior exposure to aversive stimuli or stressors changes behavioral responses to negative- and positive-value predictive cues.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, setting up the context for the study.

claim: A history of aversive stimuli negatively biased behavioral responses to motivationally relevant cues in mice.
source: We found that a history of aversive stimuli negatively biased behavioral responses to motivationally relevant cues in mice and that this negative bias was associated with hyperactivity in mPFC→PVT neurons during exposure to those cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by behavioral data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The negative behavioral bias induced by aversive stimuli was associated with hyperactivity in mPFC→PVT neurons during exposure to motivationally relevant cues.
source: We found that a history of aversive stimuli negatively biased behavioral responses to motivationally relevant cues in mice and that this negative bias was associated with hyperactivity in mPFC→PVT neurons during exposure to those cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by neural recording data presented in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: Optogenetic excitation of the mPFC→PVT pathway recapitulated the negative behavioral bias induced by aversive stimuli.
source: Furthermore, artificially mimicking this hyperactive response with selective optogenetic excitation of the same pathway recapitulated the negative behavioral bias induced by aversive stimuli, whereas optogenetic inactivation of mPFC→PVT neurons prevented the development of the negative bias.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic manipulation data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of mPFC→PVT neurons prevented the development of the negative bias.
source: Furthermore, artificially mimicking this hyperactive response with selective optogenetic excitation of the same pathway recapitulated the negative behavioral bias induced by aversive stimuli, whereas optogenetic inactivation of mPFC→PVT neurons prevented the development of the negative bias.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic inhibition data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Information flow within the mPFC→PVT circuit is critical for making predictions about motivationally-relevant outcomes as a function of prior experience.
source: Together, our results highlight how information flow within the mPFC→PVT circuit is critical for making predictions about motivationally-relevant outcomes as a function of prior experience.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined behavioral, recording, and optogenetic manipulation data.

claim: Both positive and negative mood affect decision making.
source: For example, both positive and negative mood affect decision making (Deldin and Levin, 1986; Wright and Bower, 1992; Bechara et al., 2000; Hockey et al., 2000; Dolan, 2002; Harding et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Prior exposure to aversive stimuli or stressors changes behavioral responses to ambiguous stimuli.
source: For example, prior exposure to aversive stimuli or stressors changes behavioral responses to ambiguous stimuli (Harding et al., 2004; Boleij et al., 2012; Rygula et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is critical for regulating cue-mediated behaviors in both appetitive and aversive domains.
source: The medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) is critical for regulating cue-mediated behaviors in both appetitive and aversive domains (Ishikawa et al., 2008; Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Sotres-Bayon and Quirk, 2010; Amemori and Graybiel, 2012; Burgos-Robles et al., 2013; Courtin et al., 2014; Sangha et al., 2014; Sparta et al., 2014; Burgos-Robles et al., 2017; Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Behavioral manifestations of appetitive and aversive conditioning correlate with changes in neural activity within the mPFC.
source: Behavioral manifestations of appetitive and aversive conditioning correlate with changes in neural activity within the mPFC (Burgos-Robles et al., 2009; Peters et al., 2009; Amemori and Graybiel, 2012; Burgos-Robles et al., 2013; Moorman and Aston-Jones, 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Pharmacological or optogenetic manipulations of mPFC alter both reward-seeking and fear-related behaviors.
source: and pharmacological or optogenetic manipulations of mPFC alter both reward-seeking and fear-related behaviors (Morgan and LeDoux, 1995; Blum et al., 2006; Corcoran and Quirk, 2007; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011; Sangha et al., 2014; Sparta et al., 2014; Bari et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mPFC has dense projections to subcortical structures involved in motivated behavior, including the paraventricular thalamus (PVT).
source: The mPFC has dense projections to subcortical structures involved in motivated behavior, including the paraventricular thalamus (PVT) (Vertes, 2004; Li and Kirouac, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: PVT is recruited by cues or contexts previously associated with rewarding or aversive outcomes.
source: Like the mPFC, PVT is recruited by cues or contexts previously associated with rewarding or aversive outcomes (Beck and Fibiger, 1995; Schiltz et al., 2007; Yasoshima et al., 2007; Choi et al., 2010; Igelstrom et al., 2010; Haight and Flagel, 2014; Hsu et al., 2014; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Kirouac, 2015; Matzeu et al., 2015; Penzo et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2016; Do-Monte et al., 2017; McNally, 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT neurons are activated by multiple forms of stressors.
source: PVT neurons are activated by multiple forms of stressors (Chastrette et al., 1991; Sharp et al., 1991; Cullinan et al., 1995; Bubser and Deutch, 1999; Spencer et al., 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT coordinates behavioral responses to stress.
source: and coordinate behavioral responses to stress (Hsu et al., 2014; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Penzo et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2016; Do-Monte et al., 2017; Beas et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT plays a role in multiple forms of stimulus-reward learning.
source: On the other hand, under conditions of opposing emotional valence, PVT plays a role in multiple forms of stimulus-reward learning and PVT neurons have been reported to show reward-modulated responses (Schiltz et al., 2005; Igelstrom et al., 2010; Martin-Fardon and Boutrel, 2012; James and Dayas, 2013; Browning et al., 2014; Haight and Flagel, 2014; Li et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT neurons have been reported to show reward-modulated responses.
source: On the other hand, under conditions of opposing emotional valence, PVT plays a role in multiple forms of stimulus-reward learning and PVT neurons have been reported to show reward-modulated responses (Schiltz et al., 2005; Igelstrom et al., 2010; Martin-Fardon and Boutrel, 2012; James and Dayas, 2013; Browning et al., 2014; Haight and Flagel, 2014; Li et al., 2016; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT is especially critical during motivational conflict.
source: Recent work suggests that PVT is especially critical during motivational conflict (Li et al., 2014; Choi and McNally, 2017; Zhu et al., 2018; Engelke et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent literature.

claim: Inhibition across the anterior–posterior axis of the PVT disrupts arbitration between appetitive and aversive behaviors when they are in conflict but has no effect when these behaviors are assessed in isolation.
source: Inhibition across the anterior–posterior axis of the PVT disrupts arbitration between appetitive and aversive behaviors when they are in conflict but has no effect when these behaviors are assessed in isolation (Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Activity in mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT suppresses both the acquisition and expression of conditioned reward seeking.
source: Moreover, activity in mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT also suppresses both the acquisition and expression of conditioned reward seeking (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mice in both air-puff and no-air-puff groups quickly learned the CS-US associations.
source: As predicted, mice in both air-puff and no-air-puff groups quickly learned the CS-US associations: they showed increases in anticipatory licking responses to the positive, sucrose-predicting cue and in the delay before sucrose arrived across conditioning sessions, while withholding licking after sampling the negative, denatonium-predicting cue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B and statistical analysis.

claim: Mice showed increases in anticipatory licking responses to the positive, sucrose-predicting cue across conditioning sessions.
source: As predicted, mice in both air-puff and no-air-puff groups quickly learned the CS-US associations: they showed increases in anticipatory licking responses to the positive, sucrose-predicting cue and in the delay before sucrose arrived across conditioning sessions, while withholding licking after sampling the negative, denatonium-predicting cue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice withheld licking after sampling the negative, denatonium-predicting cue.
source: As predicted, mice in both air-puff and no-air-puff groups quickly learned the CS-US associations: they showed increases in anticipatory licking responses to the positive, sucrose-predicting cue and in the delay before sucrose arrived across conditioning sessions, while withholding licking after sampling the negative, denatonium-predicting cue (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Mice in both no-air-puff and air-puff groups quickly re-adapted to the new associations during reversal learning.
source: During reversal learning, in which A and B contingencies were reversed, mice in both no-air-puff and air-puff groups quickly re-adapted to the new associations (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Licking rates for odor mixtures scaled with the proportion of the mixture that was the sucrose-predicting odor.
source: Licking rates for odor mixtures scaled with the proportion of the mixture that was the sucrose-predicting odor. This indicates that mice responded to parametrically varying ambiguous stimuli with smoothly varying behavioral responses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice responded to parametrically varying ambiguous stimuli with smoothly varying behavioral responses.
source: Licking rates for odor mixtures scaled with the proportion of the mixture that was the sucrose-predicting odor. This indicates that mice responded to parametrically varying ambiguous stimuli with smoothly varying behavioral responses (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Mice exposed to air puffs responded to ambiguous odor mixtures with fewer licks during the anticipatory odor and delay period.
source: Interestingly, mice exposed to air puffs responded to ambiguous odor mixtures with fewer licks during the anticipatory odor and delay period indicating that exposure to aversive stimuli biased decisions about ambiguous outcomes toward avoidance and away from approach (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Exposure to aversive stimuli biased decisions about ambiguous outcomes toward avoidance and away from approach.
source: Interestingly, mice exposed to air puffs responded to ambiguous odor mixtures with fewer licks during the anticipatory odor and delay period indicating that exposure to aversive stimuli biased decisions about ambiguous outcomes toward avoidance and away from approach (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The reduced licking to ambiguous cues in the air-puff group was evident on the first trial of the probe test and persisted throughout all probe test trials.
source: Notably, the reduced licking to ambiguous cues in the air-puff group was evident on the first trial of the probe test and persisted throughout all probe test trials (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by trial-by-trial behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The decline in responding was not due to effects of extinction in the probe test.
source: Thus, the decline in responding was not due to effects of extinction in the probe test.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that the effect was present from the first trial.

claim: Both groups showed similar extinction of responding to ambiguous cues across trials resulting from outcome omission.
source: Indeed, both groups showed similar extinction of responding to ambiguous cues across trials resulting from outcome omission.
evidence: This is supported by the statistical analysis showing no three-way interaction.

claim: 2208 mPFC neurons were recorded from 12 mice (929 neurons from 5 mice exposed to air puffs, 1279 neurons from 7 mice unexposed).
source: We recorded action potentials extracellularly from 2208 mPFC neurons in 12 mice, five exposed to air puffs (929 neurons), seven unexposed (1279 neurons), while mice performed the go/no-go discrimination task (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the dataset collected in the electrophysiology experiments.

claim: Most neurons showed firing rate increases or decreases following odor cues, largely with persistent activity that lasted beyond cue offset.
source: Most neurons showed firing rate increases or decreases following odor cues, largely with persistent activity that lasted beyond cue offset (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A large fraction of neurons (270 of 929 in mice exposed to air puffs and 325 of 1279 in mice unexposed) showed auROC values greater than 0.7 or less than 0.3.
source: A large fraction of neurons (270 of 929 in mice exposed to air puffs and 325 of 1279 in mice unexposed) showed auROC values greater than 0.7, indicating substantially greater activity for sucrose compared to denatonium trials, or values less than 0.3, indicating substantially greater activity for denatonium compared to sucrose trials (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 136 neurons were recorded from mPFC in the no-air-puff group during probe sessions.
source: We recorded from 136 neurons from mPFC in the no-air-puff group and 106 neurons from mPFC in air-puff exposed mice during the probe sessions (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the dataset collected during probe sessions.

claim: 106 neurons were recorded from mPFC in air-puff exposed mice during probe sessions.
source: We recorded from 136 neurons from mPFC in the no-air-puff group and 106 neurons from mPFC in air-puff exposed mice during the probe sessions (Figure 3).
evidence: This describes the dataset collected during probe sessions.

claim: 37 neurons in the no-air-puff group exhibited auROC discrimination between sucrose and denatonium trials greater than 0.7 or less than 0.3 during the probe sessions.
source: These populations included 37 in the no-air-puff group and 25 in the air-puff group that exhibited auROC discrimination between sucrose and denatonium trials greater than 0.7 or less than 0.3 during the probe sessions (see Figure 3A,B for two example neurons in mice unexposed or exposed to air puffs).
evidence: This describes a subset of neurons analyzed during probe sessions.

claim: 25 neurons in the air-puff group exhibited auROC discrimination between sucrose and denatonium trials greater than 0.7 or less than 0.3 during the probe sessions.
source: These populations included 37 in the no-air-puff group and 25 in the air-puff group that exhibited auROC discrimination between sucrose and denatonium trials greater than 0.7 or less than 0.3 during the probe sessions (see Figure 3A,B for two example neurons in mice unexposed or exposed to air puffs).
evidence: This describes a subset of neurons analyzed during probe sessions.

claim: 39 neurons were identified as projecting to PVT in mice unexposed to air puffs.
source: We identified 39 and 45 neurons as projecting to PVT in mice unexposed and exposed to air puffs, respectively (Figure 4D; no air puff group: 18 and 21 neurons during conditioning and probe sessions, respectively; air puff group: 35 and 10 neurons during conditioning and probe sessions, respectively).
evidence: This describes the dataset of identified corticothalamic neurons.

claim: 45 neurons were identified as projecting to PVT in mice exposed to air puffs.
source: We identified 39 and 45 neurons as projecting to PVT in mice unexposed and exposed to air puffs, respectively (Figure 4D; no air puff group: 18 and 21 neurons during conditioning and probe sessions, respectively; air puff group: 35 and 10 neurons during conditioning and probe sessions, respectively).
evidence: This describes the dataset of identified corticothalamic neurons.

claim: 43% of mPFC→PVT neurons recorded from mice in the air puff group showed firing rate changes in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning.
source: We found that 43% of mPFC→PVT neurons recorded from mice in the air puff group showed firing rate changes (5 of 35 neurons with increases and 10 of 35 neurons with decreases) in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: 5 of 35 mPFC→PVT neurons showed increases in firing rate in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning.
source: We found that 43% of mPFC→PVT neurons recorded from mice in the air puff group showed firing rate changes (5 of 35 neurons with increases and 10 of 35 neurons with decreases) in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: 10 of 35 mPFC→PVT neurons showed decreases in firing rate in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning.
source: We found that 43% of mPFC→PVT neurons recorded from mice in the air puff group showed firing rate changes (5 of 35 neurons with increases and 10 of 35 neurons with decreases) in response to air-puff-predicting stimuli during conditioning (Figure 4E–G).
evidence: This is supported by neural recording data shown in Figure 4E-G.

claim: mPFC→PVT neurons, thought to be involved in behavioral responses to aversive-predicting stimuli, are indeed modulated by those stimuli.
source: This demonstrates that mPFC→PVT neurons, thought to be involved in behavioral responses to aversive-predicting stimuli, are indeed modulated by those stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the neural recording data showing responses to air-puff-predicting stimuli.

claim: During the probe test, ChR2 mice showed a reduction in response to denatonium- and sucrose-predictive cues and ambiguous cues in the trials in which light was delivered in a frequency-dependent manner.
source: During the subsequent probe test, ChR2 mice showed a reduction in response to denatonium- and sucrose-predictive cues and ambiguous cues in the trials in which light was delivered in a frequency-dependent manner, whereas eYFP mice that received the same treatment responded equally in trials with or without light delivery (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: eYFP mice that received the same treatment responded equally in trials with or without light delivery.
source: During the subsequent probe test, ChR2 mice showed a reduction in response to denatonium- and sucrose-predictive cues and ambiguous cues in the trials in which light was delivered in a frequency-dependent manner, whereas eYFP mice that received the same treatment responded equally in trials with or without light delivery (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data during optogenetic stimulation shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: Stimulation of mPFC→PVT neurons did not disrupt licking for an unpredictable reward.
source: Stimulation of the same neurons did not, however, disrupt licking for an unpredictable reward.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Stimulation of mPFC→PVT axons during reward delivery did not change the number of licks in response to unexpected rewards.
source: Importantly, stimulation of mPFC→PVT axons during reward delivery at the same frequencies used in the behavioral task in half of the total number of trials did not change the number of licks in response to these rewards.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Uncued licking is not altered by optogenetic excitation of mPFC→PVT cells.
source: Thus, uncued licking is not altered by optogenetic excitation of mPFC→PVT cells and the optogenetic effects are not due to a light-induced impairment in licking in general.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing no effect on uncued licking.

claim: The optogenetic effects are not due to a light-induced impairment in licking in general.
source: Thus, uncued licking is not altered by optogenetic excitation of mPFC→PVT cells and the optogenetic effects are not due to a light-induced impairment in licking in general.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the behavioral data showing no effect on uncued licking.

claim: During the probe test, mice expressing EYFP showed a reduction in response to denatonium- and sucrose-predictive cues and ambiguous cues compared to mice expressing eNpHR3.0-EYFP.
source: During the probe test, mice expressing EYFP showed a reduction in response to denatonium- and sucrose-predictive cues and ambiguous cues in the trials compared to mice expressing eNpHR3.0-EYFP (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data during optogenetic inhibition shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Cognitive processes play an important role in generating affective states, and these affective states influence cognitive functioning by inducing attentional, memory, and judgment biases.
source: Cognitive processes—appraisals of stimuli, events and situations—play an important role in generating affective states, and these affective states influence cognitive functioning by inducing attentional, memory, and judgment biases (Lerner and Keltner, 2000; Haselton et al., 2009; Harding et al., 2004; Enkel et al., 2010; Rygula et al., 2012; Papciak et al., 2013; Rygula et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2014; Rygula et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The mPFC has long been implicated in adaptive responding by signaling information about expected outcome and by regulating sensitivity to reward and punishment.
source: Among brain regions that are engaged in affective processing, the mPFC has long been implicated in adaptive responding by signaling information about expected outcome and by regulating sensitivity to reward and punishment (Holland and Gallagher, 2004; Luk and Wallis, 2009; Alexander and Brown, 2011; Del Arco et al., 2017; Orsini et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Firing rates in mPFC neurons reflect cue-evoked expectations for aversion- and reward-predictive cues and were enhanced in mice exposed to aversive stimuli.
source: Here, we found that firing rates in mPFC neurons reflect cue-evoked expectations for aversion- and reward-predictive cues and were enhanced in mice exposed to aversive stimuli, which correlates with a reduction in anticipatory responses to the same stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the neural recording findings from the study.

claim: Enhanced firing rates in mPFC neurons in mice exposed to aversive stimuli correlate with a reduction in anticipatory responses to the same stimuli.
source: Here, we found that firing rates in mPFC neurons reflect cue-evoked expectations for aversion- and reward-predictive cues and were enhanced in mice exposed to aversive stimuli, which correlates with a reduction in anticipatory responses to the same stimuli.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the correlation between neural and behavioral data.

claim: Negative events can bias decisions by altering the activity of mPFC neurons.
source: These observations are consistent with a negative bias and suggest that negative events can bias decisions by altering the activity of mPFC neurons.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The prefrontal network is implicated in the pathophysiology of affective disorders.
source: Several studies have implicated the prefrontal network in the pathophysiology of affective disorders (Phillips et al., 2003; Drevets et al., 2008)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chronic stress has profound detrimental effects on the anatomy and physiology of mPFC neurons.
source: and chronic stress—a crucial factor in increasing the risk of developing affective disorders—has profound detrimental effects on the anatomy and physiology of mPFC neurons (Wellman, 2001; Cook and Wellman, 2004; Radley et al., 2004; Liston et al., 2006; Radley et al., 2006; Cerqueira et al., 2007; Wei et al., 2007; Liu and Aghajanian, 2008; Radley et al., 2008; Goldwater et al., 2009; Yuen et al., 2012; Adhikari et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Chronic stress induces significant regression of the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons in mPFC.
source: For example, chronic stress induces significant regression of the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons in mPFC (Cook and Wellman, 2004; Radley et al., 2004; Liston et al., 2006; Goldwater et al., 2009), which may in turn impact mPFC function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Regression of apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons in mPFC may impact mPFC function.
source: For example, chronic stress induces significant regression of the apical dendrites of pyramidal neurons in mPFC (Cook and Wellman, 2004; Radley et al., 2004; Liston et al., 2006; Goldwater et al., 2009), which may in turn impact mPFC function.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on anatomical changes.

claim: The mPFC densely projects to subcortical structures relevant for the behavioral task, including PVT, amygdala, hippocampus, and nucleus accumbens.
source: The mPFC densely projects to subcortical structures relevant for our behavioral task, including PVT, amygdala, hippocampus, and nucleus accumbens (Vertes, 2004; Li and Kirouac, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior anatomical studies.

claim: PVT has long been considered a stress detector and implicated in the emergence of adaptive responding to stress.
source: Among all brain regions that receive strong projections from the mPFC, PVT has long been considered a stress detector and implicated in the emergence of adaptive responding to stress (Chastrette et al., 1991; Sharp et al., 1991; Cullinan et al., 1995; Bubser and Deutch, 1999; Spencer et al., 2004; Hsu et al., 2014; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Penzo et al., 2015; Zhu et al., 2016; Do-Monte et al., 2017; Beas et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: PVT has been considered a potential mediator of motivated behavior responding to both food- and drug-associated cues.
source: At the same time, PVT has also been considered a potential mediator of motivated behavior responding to both food- and drug-associated cues (Schiltz et al., 2005; Igelstrom et al., 2010; Martin-Fardon and Boutrel, 2012; James and Dayas, 2013; Browning et al., 2014; Haight and Flagel, 2014; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT maintain cue-evoked expectations for motivationally-relevant outcomes and their neural activity was enhanced in mice exposed to aversive stimuli.
source: Consistent with these findings that place PVT in a position to integrate information about positive and negative motivationally relevant cues and translate it into adaptive behavioral responses (McNally, 2021), we found that mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT maintain cue-evoked expectations for motivationally-relevant outcomes and their neural activity was enhanced in mice exposed to aversive stimuli.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings on corticothalamic neurons.

claim: The experimental design cannot rule out the influence of context-derived motivational conflict on the observed behavioral outcome.
source: A feature of our experimental design is worth comment. In our experiments, mice were exposed to aversive stimuli in the same context in which they received motivationally-relevant cues. This design cannot rule out the influence of context-derived motivational conflict on the observed behavioral outcome.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation in the experimental design.

claim: PVT is important for behavioral control when appetitive and aversive behaviors are elicited at the same time and the animal must select between them.
source: PVT seems important for behavioral control when appetitive and aversive behaviors are elicited at the same time and the animal must select between them (Li et al., 2014; Choi and McNally, 2017; Zhu et al., 2018; Choi et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: By mimicking the increased response of mPFC→PVT neurons induced by exposure to aversive stimuli, a reduction in anticipatory responses to the predictive cues was observed.
source: By mimicking the increased response of mPFC→PVT neurons induced by exposure to aversive stimuli, we observed a reduction in anticipatory responses to the predictive cues.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic stimulation findings.

claim: Selective inhibition of the mPFC→PVT pathway prevented the formation of negative biases.
source: By contrast, selective inhibition of this pathway prevented the formation of negative biases.
evidence: This is a summary of the optogenetic inhibition findings.

claim: Information about cue interpretation is transferred from mPFC to PVT and this pathway is crucial for adaptive responding toward those stimuli as a function of previous experience.
source: These findings suggest that information about cue interpretation is transferred from mPFC to PVT and this pathway is crucial for adaptive responding toward those stimuli as a function of previous experience.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the combined findings from the study.

claim: Activity in mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT suppresses both the acquisition and expression of conditioned reward seeking.
source: These results are also consistent with a recent study showing that activity in mPFC neurons projecting to the PVT suppresses both the acquisition and expression of conditioned reward seeking (Otis et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature and is consistent with the current findings.

claim: There are two genetically, anatomically, and functionally distinct cell types across the anteroposterior axis of the PVT.
source: Based on recent evidence showing two genetically, anatomically, and functionally distinct cell types across the anteroposterior axis of the PVT (Gao et al., 2020), it will be interesting to investigate in future studies whether the information from mPFC is transferred to anatomically or molecularly segregated cell types or projection-specific neurons within the PVT.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: Signals from mPFC to PVT inputs propagate onto PVT projections to nucleus accumbens neurons.
source: Indeed, signals from mPFC to PVT inputs have been recently shown to propagate onto PVT projections to nucleus accumbens neurons (Otis et al., 2019)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to recent literature.

claim: mPFC to PVT signals are responsible for influencing reward seeking by adjusting a multiplexed reward signal in downstream PVT→nucleus accumbens neurons.
source: and are responsible for influencing reward seeking by adjusting a multiplexed reward signal in downstream PVT→nucleus accumbens neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the citation to Otis et al., 2019.

claim: Adaptive tuning of the mPFC→PVT network is modulated by ascending monoaminergic systems.
source: Adaptive tuning of this network is modulated by ascending monoaminergic systems (Arnsten et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Maladaptive changes of monoaminergic systems have been implicated in cognitive deficits associated with several affective disorders.
source: and maladaptive changes of these systems has been implicated in cognitive deficits associated with several affective disorders (Enkel et al., 2010; Kukolja et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Acute pharmacological stimulation of the serotonergic and dopaminergic systems has been shown to influence cognitive bias in rodents.
source: For example, acute pharmacological stimulation of the serotonergic and dopaminergic systems has been shown to influence cognitive bias in rodents (Rygula et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Citalopram and amphetamine both induced a positive cognitive processing bias in rodents.
source: In particular, citalopram, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, and amphetamine, a powerful psychostimulant, both induced a positive cognitive processing bias (Rygula et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Negative cognitive bias lies at the core of the pathophysiology of several affective disorders.
source: Those results are important from a clinical point of view, knowing that negative cognitive bias lies at the core of the pathophysiology of several affective disorders and it has been extensively studied in humans (Wright and Bower, 1992; MacLeod and Byrne, 1996; Beck, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Patients with anxiety and depression interpret ambiguous information with a negative bias.
